title: Sample-Adaptive Latent Rewards for Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Post-Training

paper.title: Sample-Adaptive Latent Rewards for Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Post-Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Latent reward models can supervise visual diffusion models without decoding intermediate states into pixel space. This makes alignment with human preferences more efficient. However, existing latent reward models output only scalar scores. They do not estimate the uncertainty of each prediction. The generator therefore cannot determine which feedback is reliable. This can drive optimization in the wrong direction and lead to reward hacking.
We propose SURE , a unified latent-space framework for image and video diffusion models. It learns reward distributions and directly uses their reliability to guide dense post-training. First, we propose sample-adaptive latent reward model ( SURE-LRM ). It predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent. Its mean predicts the reward score. Its variance reflect the uncertainty of prediction without human annotation. The learned distribution then guides post-training through uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning ( SURE-REFL ). This method provides uncertainty-guided dense feedback along the denoising trajectory. At selected transitions, SURE-REFL queries the frozen SURE-LRM . It converts detached variance into reliability weights for samples at the same transition. Each weighted reward is backpropagated only through its local transition. The entire process remains in latent space and requires neither pixel-space decoding nor the full denoising graph.
Experiments show that SURE-LRM improves preference prediction over strong baselines. SURE-REFL achieves the sota performance among various metrics and further improves optimization stability. It also achieves the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores among the evaluated methods.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Post-training has become central to aligning visual diffusion models with human preferences. Existing pipelines commonly evaluate preference signals on decoded RGB outputs, introducing repeated VAE decoding into the feedback loop ( Prabhudesai et al. 2023 ; Black et al. 2024 ; Liu et al. 2025a ) . Diffusion-native reward models instead score noisy latents directly, avoiding this decoding cost and making intermediate-state supervision possible ( Zhang et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2026a ) . However, existing latent rewards typically output only a scalar score. DiNa-LRM further advances this direction by explicitly considering the noise structure of diffusion models ( Liu et al. 2026 ) . Rather than learning rewards only from clean latents, it trains a timestep-conditioned reward model on states with different noise levels. It takes the denoising scheduler as uncertainty into preference learning. Higher-noise states are assigned greater uncertainty as they contain less information. However, noise level alone does not fully determine the reliability of a reward prediction. DiNa-LRM assigns the same uncertainty to all latent samples at the same timestep. In practice, reward difficulty also depends on the specific content being evaluated. At a fixed noise level, one latent may already reveal a clear subject, while another may remain ambiguous. A relatively noisy but easy sample may therefore support a more reliable prediction than a lower-noise but difficult sample. A second limitation concerns how uncertainty is used. In DiNa-LRM, noise-dependent uncertainty supports reward model training, but it is not retained for generator optimization. However, a reward prediction with high uncertainty should have less influence than a reliable prediction. Since unreliable local feedback may repeatedly affect generator updates, even leds to reward hacking. Figure 1: Comparison of reward feedback paradigms. The mean-only latent rewards cannot express predictive uncertainty. SURE-LRM predicts a latent reward and sample-adaptive uncertainty. REFL fails to leverage predictive uncertainty, while SURE-REFL uses detached uncertainty to control dense local feedback. To address these limitations, we propose SURE , a unified framework for sample-adaptive latent reward uncertainty modeling and diffusion post-training. The framework consists of two parts, SURE-LRM and SURE-REFL . First, SURE-LRM builds upon the diffusion uncertainty prior to predict residual uncertainty conditioned on the latent, prompt, and timestep. It predicts a mean reward and sample-dependent variance using a heteroscedastic preference objective learned from standard pairwise preferences without additional uncertainty or confidence annotations. Variance regularization controls uncertainty inflation, while margin regularization maintains score separation. Additionally, SURE-REFL leverages the frozen SURE-LRM directly in latent space. It queries multiple denoising transitions and backpropagates each reward only through its local transition. Detached uncertainty controls the relative contribution of feedback by comparing samples evaluated at the same transition for both image and video generators. Thus, reward learning and generator alignment remain in latent space without VAE decoding or retention of the full denoising graph. Experiments indicate SURE-LRM achieves state of art preference prediction over multi-backbones as latent reward model. SURE-REFL delivers meaningful performance across diverse evaluation metrics on both image and video post-training. Moreover, SURE-REFL exhibits more stable training behavior and reduced reward hacking. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formulate sample-adaptive reward uncertainty in latent space through a preference model. We derive its variance gradients to show how does it provides an uncertainty-learning signal. • We propose SURE-LRM , which learns sample-adaptive latent reward uncertainty from standard pairwise preferences without additional confidence annotations. • We develop SURE-REFL , a unified image–video post-training method that allocates dense latent feedback using detached uncertainty without VAE decoding. • Experiments show state-of-the-art post-training performance in the evaluated settings across both image backbones and video backbone.

sections.heading: Visual reward models.
sections.text: Early learned visual rewards map decoded image–text pairs to scalar utilities. ImageReward trains such a scorer from human comparisons ( Xu et al. 2023 ) , while PickScore, HPSv2, and MPS expand user-preference data, cross-distribution evaluation, or multi-dimensional assessment ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2024 ) . More recent VLM-based systems increase model and task coverage: UnifiedReward evaluates both multimodal understanding and generation, UnifiedReward-Think adds explicit reward reasoning, and HPSv3 combines a larger preference corpus with uncertainty-aware ranking ( Wang et al. 2025b ; Wang et al. 2025a ; Ma et al. 2025 ) . These pixel-space evaluators require VAE decoding, which is costly when rewards are queried at many denoising states. Diffusion-native approaches instead evaluate intermediate latents. LRM repurposes diffusion features to score arbitrary noisy states for step-level preference optimization ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) ; DiNa-LRM learns a general-purpose latent reward with a noise-calibrated Thurstone likelihood and multi-noise inference ( Liu et al. 2026 ) ; and DRM employs a diffusion backbone for stepwise guidance in group relative policy optimization (GRPO) and sampling ( Zhang et al. 2026a ) . These methods establish that noisy states are scoreable, but they do not expose sample-specific reward reliability to the downstream optimizer.

sections.heading: Diffusion preference optimization.
sections.text: Post-training methods differ in how they convert feedback into generator updates. AlignProp and DRaFT propagate gradients from differentiable rewards through full or truncated denoising graphs ( Prabhudesai et al. 2023 ; Clark et al. 2024 ) . DDPO casts denoising as a multi-step Markov decision process and applies policy-gradient reinforcement learning to terminal rewards ( Black et al. 2024 ) , whereas Diffusion-DPO directly optimizes offline pairwise preferences through a diffusion-specific DPO objective ( Wallace et al. 2024 ) . Building on group relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , Flow-GRPO extends online optimization to flow-matching models ( Liu et al. 2025a ) , DanceGRPO applies it across image and video generation tasks ( Xue et al. 2025 ) , and ViPO redistributes scalar feedback into spatially and temporally structured advantages ( Ni et al. 2026 ) . For video generation, Process Reward Feedback Learning (PRFL) repurposes a pretrained video generator as a noisy-latent process reward model and backpropagates preference feedback through the denoising chain without VAE decoding ( Mi et al. 2025 ) . These methods improve the optimization or credit-assignment rule, but dense feedback additionally requires the reliability of intermediate reward predictions to be estimated and used during generator updates.

sections.heading: Uncertainty-aware reward learning.
sections.text: Confidence-aware reward optimization shows that visual-model fine-tuning can benefit from attenuating unreliable reward signals ( Kim et al. 2024 ) , while probabilistic uncertain reward modeling represents reward as a distribution rather than a point estimate ( Sun et al. 2026 ) . We bring this principle to diffusion-native visual rewards: SURE-LRM learns sample-dependent relative reliability from ordinary pairwise preferences, and SURE-REFL uses it to weight dense local feedback among states evaluated at the same transition.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: To enable uncertainty-aware reward modeling and efficient reward-guided post-training in latent space, we first develop SURE-LRM , which predicts a preference score together with sample-adaptive uncertainty for each noisy latent. We then freeze the reward model and introduce SURE-REFL to allocate dense reward feedback across denoising transitions using detached uncertainty. Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the two components, respectively. Due to space constraints, the detailed proof is provided in the supplementary material. Figure 2: Overview of SURE-LRM . The latent reward backbone predicts a mean reward and sample-adaptive residual uncertainty from the noisy latent, prompt, and timestep. The residual is combined with the noise-dependent prior to form the total predictive variance.

sections.heading: Unified model architecture.
sections.text: Across image and video modalities, SURE-LRM reuses the DiT backbone of the corresponding generator as its latent feature encoder, providing a unified architecture that directly processes noisy latents, prompts, and timesteps without VAE decoding. For images, learned queries aggregate multi-layer visual–text features; for videos, a query-attention pooler summarizes intermediate spatiotemporal features from the Wan DiT. A shared two-output projection maps the aggregated representation to the mean reward μ \mu and residual-variance parameter a a . Backbone-specific feature layers, query counts, and projection dimensions are provided in the supplementary material.

Each reward is backpropagated only through its local transition.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We first evaluate SURE-LRM on four image preference benchmarks: ImageReward ( Xu et al. 2023 ) , HPD v2 ( Wu et al. 2023 ) , HPD v3 ( Ma et al. 2025 ) , and GenAI-Bench ( Jiang et al. 2024 ) . We compare it with CLIP-based rewards (ImageReward, PickScore, HPSv2, and MPS), VLM-based rewards (UnifiedReward, UnifiedReward-Think, and HPSv3), and diffusion-based rewards (LRM and DiNa-LRM) ( Xu et al. 2023 ; Kirstain et al. 2023 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2025b ; Wang et al. 2025a ; Ma et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; Liu et al. 2026 ) . For video preference prediction, we use VisionRewardDB ( Xu et al. 2026 ) and a held-out split of T2V Ranking Human Preferences ( Datapoint AI 2026 ) ; its source videos were introduced with VideoScore2 ( He et al. 2025 ) . The baselines cover image reward models and video-specific reward models: HPSv2.1, ImageReward, PickScore, VideoScore, VideoReward, Q-Insight, UnifiedReward-Think, and VisionReward ( HPSv2 Project 2024 ; Xu et al. 2023 ; Kirstain et al. 2023 ; He et al. 2024 ; Liu et al. 2025b ; Li et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025a ; Xu et al. 2026 ) . Published VisionRewardDB results follow the tie-excluded protocol reported by VQ-Insight ( Zhang et al. 2026b ) . For image post-training, we test SD3.5-Medium, Z-Image-Turbo, and FLUX.1-dev. The baselines are Flow-GRPO, LPO, ViPO, and DiNa-LRM ( Liu et al. 2025a ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; Ni et al. 2026 ; Liu et al. 2026 ) . We report HPSv2.1, ImageReward, and PickScore ( HPSv2 Project 2024 ; Xu et al. 2023 ; Kirstain et al. 2023 ) . For video, we post-train Wan2.1-480P-T2V-14B ( Team Wan et al. 2025 ) and compare with DanceGRPO, ViPO, VideoDPO, and HY-PRFL on VBench ( Xue et al. 2025 ; Ni et al. 2026 ; Liu et al. 2025c ; Mi et al. 2025 ; Huang et al. 2024 ) . The supplementary material provides the human study, computational-cost comparison, and full implementation details.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: All variants of a backbone use matched prompts, sampling budgets, resolutions, and metric implementations. For VisionRewardDB, we exclude 180 human-tie pairs and evaluate the remaining 820 comparisons. Published VisionRewardDB baseline results use the same tie-excluded protocol, while the remaining entries are obtained with our evaluation pipeline. Results for our method in Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 use three random seeds. Each seed is evaluated once, and we report the mean across the three runs. SURE-REFL queries the frozen SURE-LRM at selected denoising transitions and backpropagates through each local transition. Dataset construction, checkpoint identifiers, optimization hyperparameters, sampling schedules, and compute resources are provided in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Uncertainty reliability.
sections.text: At a fixed transition, all samples share the same noise-dependent prior. Their variance differences therefore come from the learned residual term. Table 2 shows that incorrect rankings have 24.26% higher residual variance on average. Predicted variance identifies ranking errors with an AUROC of 0.6941, and retaining the lowest-variance half raises pairwise accuracy from 79.40% to 90.10%. It also agrees with human confidence under both u u conditions. These results show that the learned variance contains useful information about relative reward reliability, which motivates its use in SURE-REFL . Because these pairs appeared during training, we treat this evidence as an in-distribution diagnostic rather than held-out calibration. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: SURE unifies uncertainty-aware latent reward learning and dense visual-model alignment. SURE-LRM learns candidate-dependent reward variance directly from pairwise preferences, and SURE-REFL converts this uncertainty into bounded, detached weights for local image and video post-training. SURE-LRM improves matched-backbone pairwise accuracy over DiNa-LRM, while SURE-REFL yields consistent image-generation gains and the highest VBench aggregate scores among the compared methods. Future work should examine uncertainty calibration under distribution shift and extend the evaluation to additional video domains. Overall, the results support treating state-specific reliability and local trajectory feedback as first-class properties of latent rewards used for visual alignment.

This makes alignment with human preferences more efficient. However, existing latent reward models output only scalar scores. They do not estimate the uncertainty of each prediction. The generator therefore cannot determine which feedback is reliable. This can drive optimization in the wrong direction and lead to reward hacking. We propose SURE , a unified latent-space framework for image and video diffusion models. It learns reward distributions and directly uses their reliability to guide dense post-training. First, we propose sample-adaptive latent reward model ( SURE-LRM ). It predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent. Its mean predicts the reward score. Its variance reflect the uncertainty of prediction without human annotation. The learned distribution then guides post-training through uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning ( SURE-REFL ). This method provides uncertainty-guided dense feedback along the denoising trajectory. At selected transitions, SURE-REFL queries the frozen SURE-LRM . It converts detached variance into reliability weights for samples at the same transition. Each weighted reward is backpropagated only through its local transition. The entire process remains in latent space and requires neither pixel-space decoding nor the full denoising graph. Experiments show that SURE-LRM improves preference prediction over strong baselines. SURE-REFL achieves the sota performance among various metrics and further improves optimization stability. It also achieves the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores among the evaluated methods. 1 University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China 2 Institute of Artificial Intelligence, China Telecom (TeleAI), Shanghai, China 3 Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China rui.li@mail.ustc.edu.cn, xuelong_li@ieee.org 1 Introduction Post-training has become central to aligning visual diffusion models with human preferences. Existing pipelines commonly evaluate preference signals on decoded RGB outputs, introducing repeated VAE decoding into the feedback loop ( Prabhudesai et al. 2023 ; Black et al. 2024 ; Liu et al. 2025a ) . Diffusion-native reward models instead score noisy latents directly, avoiding this decoding cost and making intermediate-state supervision possible ( Zhang et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2026a ) . However, existing latent rewards typically output only a scalar score. DiNa-LRM further advances this direction by explicitly considering the noise structure of diffusion models ( Liu et al. 2026 ) . Rather than learning rewards only from clean latents, it trains a timestep-conditioned reward model on states with different noise levels. It takes the denoising scheduler as uncertainty into preference learning. Higher-noise states are assigned greater uncertainty as they contain less information. However, noise level alone does not fully determine the reliability of a reward prediction. DiNa-LRM assigns the same uncertainty to all latent samples at the same timestep. In practice, reward difficulty also depends on the specific content being evaluated. At a fixed noise level, one latent may already reveal a clear subject, while another may remain ambiguous. A relatively noisy but easy sample may therefore support a more reliable prediction than a lower-noise but difficult sample. A second limitation concerns how uncertainty is used. In DiNa-LRM, noise-dependent uncertainty supports reward model training, but it is not retained for generator optimization. However, a reward prediction with high uncertainty should have less influence than a reliable prediction. Since unreliable local feedback may repeatedly affect generator updates, even leds to reward hacking. Figure 1: Comparison of reward feedback paradigms. The mean-only latent rewards cannot express predictive uncertainty. SURE-LRM predicts a latent reward and sample-adaptive uncertainty. REFL fails to leverage predictive uncertainty, while SURE-REFL uses detached uncertainty to control dense local feedback. To address these limitations, we propose SURE , a unified framework for sample-adaptive latent reward uncertainty modeling and diffusion post-training. The framework consists of two parts, SURE-LRM and SURE-REFL . First, SURE-LRM builds upon the diffusion uncertainty prior to predict residual uncertainty conditioned on the latent, prompt, and timestep. It predicts a mean reward and sample-dependent variance using a heteroscedastic preference objective learned from standard pairwise preferences without additional uncertainty or confidence annotations. Variance regularization controls uncertainty inflation, while margin regularization maintains score separation. Additionally, SURE-REFL leverages the frozen SURE-LRM directly in latent space. It queries multiple denoising transitions and backpropagates each reward only through its local transition. Detached uncertainty controls the relative contribution of feedback by comparing samples evaluated at the same transition for both image and video generators. Thus, reward learning and generator alignment remain in latent space without VAE decoding or retention of the full denoising graph. Experiments indicate SURE-LRM achieves state of art preference prediction over multi-backbones as latent reward model. SURE-REFL delivers meaningful performance across diverse evaluation metrics on both image and video post-training. Moreover, SURE-REFL exhibits more stable training behavior and reduced reward hacking. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formulate sample-adaptive reward uncertainty in latent space through a preference model. We derive its variance gradients to show how does it provides an uncertainty-learning signal. • We propose SURE-LRM , which learns sample-adaptive latent reward uncertainty from standard pairwise preferences without additional confidence annotations. • We develop SURE-REFL , a unified image–video post-training method that allocates dense latent feedback using detached uncertainty without VAE decoding. • Experiments show state-of-the-art post-training performance in the evaluated settings across both image backbones and video backbone. 2 Related Work Visual reward models. Early learned visual rewards map decoded image–text pairs to scalar utilities. ImageReward trains such a scorer from human comparisons ( Xu et al. 2023 ) , while PickScore, HPSv2, and MPS expand user-preference data, cross-distribution evaluation, or multi-dimensional assessment ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2024 ) . More recent VLM-based systems increase model and task coverage: UnifiedReward evaluates both multimodal understanding and generation, UnifiedReward-Think adds explicit reward reasoning, and HPSv3 combines a larger preference corpus with uncertainty-aware ranking ( Wang et al. 2025b ; Wang et al. 2025a ; Ma et al. 2025 ) . These pixel-space evaluators require VAE decoding, which is costly when rewards are queried at many denoising states. Diffusion-native approaches instead evaluate intermediate latents. LRM repurposes diffusion features to score arbitrary noisy states for step-level preference optimization ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) ; DiNa-LRM learns a general-purpose latent reward with a noise-calibrated Thurstone likelihood and multi-noise inference ( Liu et al. 2026 ) ; and DRM employs a diffusion backbone for stepwise guidance in group relative policy optimization (GRPO) and sampling ( Zhang et al. 2026a ) . These methods establish that noisy states are scoreable, but they do not expose sample-specific reward reliability to the downstream optimizer. Diffusion preference optimization. Post-training methods differ in how they convert feedback into generator updates. AlignProp and DRaFT propagate gradients from differentiable rewards through full or truncated denoising graphs ( Prabhudesai et al. 2023 ; Clark et al. 2024 ) . DDPO casts denoising as a multi-step Markov decision process and applies policy-gradient reinforcement learning to terminal rewards ( Black et al. 2024 ) , whereas Diffusion-DPO directly optimizes offline pairwise preferences through a diffusion-specific DPO objective ( Wallace et al. 2024 ) . Building on group relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , Flow-GRPO extends online optimization to flow-matching models ( Liu et al. 2025a ) , DanceGRPO applies it across image and video generation tasks ( Xue et al. 2025 ) , and ViPO redistributes scalar feedback into spatially and temporally structured advantages ( Ni et al. 2026 ) . For video generation, Process Reward Feedback Learning (PRFL) repurposes a pretrained video generator as a noisy-latent process reward model and backpropagates preference feedback through the denoising chain without VAE decoding ( Mi et al. 2025 ) . These methods improve the optimization or credit-assignment rule, but dense feedback additionally requires the reliability of intermediate reward predictions to be estimated and used during generator updates. Uncertainty-aware reward learning. Confidence-aware reward optimization shows that visual-model fine-tuning can benefit from attenuating unreliable reward signals ( Kim et al. 2024 ) , while probabilistic uncertain reward modeling represents reward as a distribution rather than a point estimate ( Sun et al. 2026 ) . We bring this principle to diffusion-native visual rewards: SURE-LRM learns sample-dependent relative reliability from ordinary pairwise preferences, and SURE-REFL uses it to weight dense local feedback among states evaluated at the same transition. 3 Method To enable uncertainty-aware reward modeling and efficient reward-guided post-training in latent space, we first develop SURE-LRM , which predicts a preference score together with sample-adaptive uncertainty for each noisy latent. We then freeze the reward model and introduce SURE-REFL to allocate dense reward feedback across denoising transitions using detached uncertainty. The latent reward backbone predicts a mean reward and sample-adaptive residual uncertainty from the noisy latent, prompt, and timestep. SURE-LRM learns candidate-dependent reward variance directly from pairwise preferences, and SURE-REFL converts this uncertainty into bounded, detached weights for local image and video post-training. SURE-LRM improves matched-backbone pairwise accuracy over DiNa-LRM, while SURE-REFL yields consistent image-generation gains and the highest VBench aggregate scores among the compared methods.
